extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and evaluating novels focused on the relation between plot and character and on the use of fantasy/prophetic elements; includes examples and anti-patterns from classic novelists. Useful for creative-writing practice and literary criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot ought to cause surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: “This shock, followed by the feeling, ‘Oh, that’s all right,’ is a sign that all is well with the plot: characters, to be real, ought to run smoothly, but a plot ought to cause surprise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good plot produces genuine shocks that nevertheless resolve into a sense of rightness. Example: the horse‑whipping of Dr. Shrapnel in Beauchamp’s Career is an incident that surprises readers and characters and transforms the book’s world. Avoid plots that never surprise or that manufacture surprise in an unconvincing way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident should spring from character and alter that character
rubrics_metrics.description: “Incident springs out of character, and having occurred it alters that character.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot events should be motivated by characters' natures and should have consequential effects on those characters. Contrivances are acceptable when they arise from character and change them (Meredithian contrivances as 'doors' through which the book passes). Avoid arbitrary incidents that do not relate to character motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must run smoothly (internal consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Characters, to be real, ought to run smoothly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain coherent, continuous inner lives for characters so that their behavior feels plausible. Even when plot shocks occur, characters’ internal consistency helps readers accept changes. Anti-pattern: characters who behave erratically solely to serve the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contrivances: must spring from characters and react upon them
rubrics_metrics.description: Meredith’s contrivances are often 'delightful, sometimes touching, always unexpected' and act as doors through which the book emerges 'in an altered form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrivances can be artful and productive if they derive from character situations and have meaningful repercussions. They should not feel like theatrical gimmicks detached from psychological truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of inner change as a valid plot device (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meredith conceals Laetitia Dale’s mental change so that the late revelation gives a dramatic effect: 'Meredith has concealed the change. It would have spoiled his high comedy if we had been kept in touch with it throughout.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiding a character’s inner development can be dramatically effective (creates a late reveal), but risks damaging character credibility if it violates previously established narrative obligations (example: Charlotte Brontë’s concealment in Villette which weakens Lucy Snowe’s moral integrity). Use concealment when it preserves the work’s tone and does not betray the character’s voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance plot causality and the novel’s medium — do not force characters to acquiesce
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy 'arranges events with emphasis on causality' so strongly that characters are 'ordered to acquiesce in its requirements,' which weakens their reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over‑emphasizing plot causality to the point characters become mere instruments of fate. Consider the novel’s capacity to contain other modes (poetry, interior life) rather than canalizing everything into action. Anti-pattern: demanding more contribution from characters than the medium can sustain, resulting in 'dry and thin' figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical or feeble endings that kill character vitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all novels are feeble at the end because 'the novelist has to round things off, and usually the characters go dead while he is at work.' Death and marriage are common convenient devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endings should preserve the sense of living character and avoid forcing every earlier incidental element to contribute artificially to a dénouement. Beware of concluding solely by convenient conventions (death/marriage) or by letting logic override 'flesh and blood.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot is the novel’s logical/intellectual aspect but need not always dominate; allow organic growth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The plot, then, is the novel in its logical intellectual aspect... He plans his book beforehand: or anyhow he stands above it, his interest in cause and effect give him an air of predetermination.” Yet Gide proposes letting reality dictate and the book grow without plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize plot as a planning tool but be open to non‑planned, organic composition. Some novels benefit from authorial oversight and causal architecture; others (modern experiments) succeed by admitting contingency and growth. Choose the approach suited to the book’s aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment: fragmentary or self‑reflexive structures can replace unified plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Gide’s Les Faux Monnayeurs contains plot‑fragments, diaries, and a novelist‑character (Edouard) whose diary forms the bulk of the book; the work mixes truth in life and truth in art and 'breaks up' plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fragmentation, metafictional devices, and mixing documentary material (diary, authorial voice) are legitimate alternatives to tightly knit plots. Such forms aim to combine different 'truths' and to let reality intrude; they may bore some readers but can be stimulating when done with purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelists must reconcile two forces: human beings and non‑human elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Central idea: 'there are in the novel two forces: human beings and a bundle of various things not human beings, and it is the novelist’s business to adjust these two forces and conciliate their claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft requires negotiating character (human complexity) and other aspects (plot, fate, fantasy, theme, idea). The successful novel balances these without allowing one to crush the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy demands an additional readerly adjustment (pay something extra)
rubrics_metrics.description: “What does fantasy ask of us? It asks us to pay something extra. It compels us to an adjustment... I must ask you first to accept my book as a whole, and secondly to accept certain things in my book.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing fantastical elements, the author must secure the reader’s willingness to accept both the overall fictive contract and particular impossible events/figures. Some readers will refuse this 'sixpence' fee; the author must judge whether the intended audience will pay it and ensure the fantastic is appropriate to the book’s tone and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fantasy from prophecy by their mythologies/gods
rubrics_metrics.description: “They are alike in having gods, and unlike in the gods they have... By their mythologies we shall distinguish these two sorts of novels.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'fantasy' for works haunted by small gods/fairies/folk mythology (Hermes, Pan, fairies); use 'prophecy' for works invoking transcendent, large‑scale deities and prophetic vision. The tonal and thematic implications differ and should guide choice of device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devices characteristic of the fantastic (limited repertory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices include: introduction of a god/ghost/angel/monkey/monster/midget/witch into ordinary life; introduction of ordinary men into no‑man’s‑land, the future, the past, the interior of the earth, the fourth dimension; dividings/divings of personality; parody or adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fantasy writers repeatedly draw on a fairly limited set of devices; fresh treatment, tone, and suitability to the book determine success. Be aware of these common devices and select/manipulate them deliberately rather than randomly.

rubrics_metrics.name: The fantastic’s characteristic effect: improvised air but can include serious character and critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy 'has an improvised air, which is the secret of their force and charm. They may contain solid character-drawing, penetrating and bitter criticism of conduct and civilization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fantastic can produce an extemporaneous, mischievous tone while still delivering serious moral or aesthetic content. Examples: Tristram Shandy (invokes 'Muddle') and Flecker’s Magic (wish‑ring). Expect divided responses—some readers thrilled, others 'choked off'—and write to the readership you intend to engage.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Meredithian (episodic) plot is an acceptable architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: A Meredithian plot 'is not a temple to the tragic or even to the comic Muse, but rather resembles a series of kiosks most artfully placed among wooded slopes,' where people reach them and 'emerge with altered aspect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic or kiosk‑like structures (discrete incidents that alter characters) are valid alternatives to tightly knit dramatic plots. They work when incidents organically reflect character and produce transformation without formal unity of a single central action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of beauty: a face of beauty should look slightly surprised
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Beauty ought to look a little surprised: it is the emotion that best suits her face... The beauty who does not look surprised, who accepts her position as her due—she reminds us too much of a prima donna.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing beauty, imbue it with a trace of surprise to avoid stiff, self‑satisfied portrayal. Small expressive details (a look of surprise) can make physical description seem lively rather than posed or prima donna‑like.
